Name: reasoning_depth_classes
Title: Shallow Words, Deep Deductions: Training-Free Per-Token Depth Allocation from Convergence Layers of Chain-of-Thought Tokens
Short Hypothesis: Chain-of-thought tokens differ sharply in the transformer depth they actually require: connective/filler/restating tokens have their next-token prediction 'converge' at shallow layers (stable under logit lens), while genuine deduction tokens keep changing through deep layers. This convergence depth is measurable online via early-layer prediction stability, forming interpretable 'reasoning depth classes.' Skipping the remaining layers for shallow-converged tokens saves compute per token without retraining and with minimal accuracy loss, and is orthogonal to token-count pruning.
Related Work: System-1.5 Reasoning and CoLa achieve per-token/per-sample depth adaptation but require self-distillation training or expensive per-sample MCTS. AdaDecode exits at intermediate layers using output confidence with a verification step for exact parity, treating all tokens uniformly by a single confidence rule. LYNX/ROM reduce token COUNT via hidden-state early-exit at reasoning cues; my prior proposals also target token-count reduction (pruning, early answer commitment, branch pruning). This proposal is distinct on two axes: (1) it reduces PER-TOKEN DEPTH rather than the number of tokens, and (2) it grounds depth allocation in a mechanistic, interpretable taxonomy of CoT tokens by their logit-lens convergence layer, yielding both a training-free controller and a scientific map of which reasoning-token roles are shallow vs deep. No prior work characterizes reasoning-token depth requirements by semantic role or exploits this taxonomy for training-free CoT compute allocation.
Abstract: Reasoning models run every chain-of-thought (CoT) token through the full transformer stack, but not all reasoning tokens need the same compute. Using the logit lens, we observe that the next-token prediction for many CoT tokens stabilizes at shallow layers and does not change through the remaining depth, whereas other tokens keep changing until late layers. We hypothesize that CoT tokens fall into interpretable 'reasoning depth classes': shallow tokens (connectives, restatements, hedging, formatting) versus deep tokens (novel deductions, arithmetic results, sub-conclusions), and that the layer at which a token's prediction converges is a reliable, online-measurable indicator of the compute it needs. We first characterize convergence depth across GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA on multiple open-weight reasoning models, correlating it with token semantic role and with each token's causal importance (via activation ablation). We then build a training-free per-token depth-allocation controller: at generation time we monitor early-layer prediction stability and, once a token's top prediction is stable across a short layer window with sufficient margin, we skip the remaining layers (propagating the converged residual with cached KV), while deep tokens receive the full stack. We evaluate accuracy versus compute (mean layers executed, FLOPs, wall-clock) against full-depth decoding, AdaDecode-style uniform confidence exit, and fixed-depth truncation, on models from 1.5B-8B. We expect 20-40% per-token compute savings at near-equal accuracy, plus a mechanistic taxonomy of reasoning-token depth requirements that complements token-count pruning and can be composed with it.
Experiments: 1. Convergence-depth characterization: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, generate full CoT on GSM8K, MATH, ProntoQA. For each CoT token, apply the logit lens (or tuned lens) at every layer and record the earliest layer after which the top-1 predicted token stays fixed with a confidence margin ('convergence layer'). Report the distribution of convergence layers and the fraction of tokens that converge early. 2. Depth-class taxonomy: Tag tokens by role using lightweight heuristics/regex (connectives, restatements, hedging/reflection markers, numeric results, operators, sub-conclusion phrases). Test whether convergence layer differs significantly by role (ANOVA / effect sizes), establishing interpretable shallow vs deep classes. 3. Causal validation: For a sampled set, ablate each token's late-layer residual contributions (layers beyond its convergence layer) and measure answer flips; shallow-converged tokens should tolerate late-layer removal far better than deep tokens. Report answer-flip rate vs convergence layer. 4. Per-token depth controller (training-free): During generation, after each layer compute the logit-lens prediction; if top-1 is unchanged for W consecutive layers with margin > tau, stop computing further layers for that token, project the current residual to logits, and cache the partial KV (using the last computed layer's key/value, with a fallback that recomputes skipped-layer KV lazily if a later token attends heavily to that position). Deep tokens run full depth. 5. Evaluation: accuracy vs mean layers executed per token (Pareto), estimated FLOPs, and wall-clock latency; baselines: full-depth CoT, AdaDecode-style single-confidence exit, fixed-depth (skip last k layers uniformly), and tuned-lens vs logit-lens variants. Metrics: accuracy, mean layers/token, FLOP reduction, latency, flip rate vs full-depth outputs. 6. Composition test: Combine depth allocation with a simple token-count early-exit (e.g., LYNX-style) to show the two savings axes are complementary (multiplicative compute reduction). 7. Ablations: stability window W and margin tau, layer at which monitoring starts, KV-cache handling strategies, per-difficulty accuracy breakdown, and cross-model/cross-dataset transfer of convergence-layer thresholds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Skipping layers per token corrupts the KV cache for skipped layers, which later tokens may need to attend to; we mitigate with lazy recomputation of KV for high-attention positions and quantify the resulting overhead and accuracy cost. 2. Logit-lens convergence may be noisy or misleading in some layers/models; we compare against tuned lens and validate against causal ablation ground truth. 3. Realizing wall-clock speedup from per-token depth skipping requires batching/kernel support; we report FLOPs and layers-executed as hardware-agnostic metrics and provide a single-sequence latency measurement as an existence proof. 4. Deep computation may sometimes only manifest in later layers even for tokens whose top-1 appeared stable early (margin masks a late flip); the margin and window guard against this and the flip-rate metric quantifies residual damage. 5. Convergence-depth thresholds may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring cheap one-time calibration; transfer is tested explicitly. 6. The semantic-role tagging is heuristic and imperfect; the taxonomy claims are supported by aggregate statistics rather than per-token labels.
